title: Adding tools and memory to the project
notes: Scout has six tools: four that look things up and two that act, with the rules for acting built into the tool.
Fake data in data/orders.json lets you test every hard case, from a late return to a carrier timeout, without real systems.
Memory keeps the recent turns plus pinned facts, like the order ID and email, that are never trimmed.

slides.title: Adding tools and memory to the project
slides.sub: Six tools, fake data you control, and memory that never loses the order number
sentences: Scout's loop runs. Now we give it everything its job needs.
That means six tools, data to test them with, and a memory that keeps what matters.
You'll also see how one sentence in a tool description can make or break a run.

slides.title: Four tools that look things up

cells: Where it is, when it arrives

note.text: These only read. Calling one twice wastes a step but does no harm.

sentences: Four of Scout's six tools look things up.
Get order finds an order by its number, or by the email address the customer ordered with.
Track parcel asks the carrier, ParcelPath, where a parcel is and when it should arrive.
Check stock tells Scout how many of a product are left, using the product's stock code.
Search policy finds the two sections of Orbit's policy that best match a question, just as you built it in Module 4.
These four only read, so calling one twice wastes a step but does no harm.

slides.title: Two tools that act

messages.label: Owen
messages.text: I've posted the jacket back. Please refund the $310.

messages.label: request_refund
messages.text: ORB-10588, $310 → status: pending_approval. Over $200 needs a person.

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: Thanks, Owen. Your $310 refund is started. As it's over $200, a member of our support team will review it.

messages.label: Owen
messages.text: Can I just talk to a person about it?

messages.label: hand_off
messages.text: Owen Hart, ORB-10588: $310 refund pending approval, wants to talk to a person. → ticket HO-1001

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: Of course. I've passed your chat to the team with a summary, ticket HO-1001.

aside.label: Rules inside the tool
aside.text: request_refund never approves over $200 by itself, however the model asks.

sentences: The other two tools change something, so they need more care.
Owen has posted his jacket back and asks for his money.
Scout calls request refund, and because it's over two hundred dollars, the tool answers pending approval.
Scout passes that on honestly: the refund is started, and a person will review it.
When Owen asks for a person, Scout calls the sixth tool, hand off, with a short summary.
The team gets a ticket with the whole story, and Owen doesn't have to repeat himself.
Notice that the approval rule lives inside the tool, so even a confused model can't skip it.

slides.title: Fake data you control
slides.lead: Real systems come later. A small file and two dictionaries let you make every case happen on demand.

rows.out: the five sample orders, with emails

aside.label: Why fake first
aside.text: A late return, a timeout, a big refund: you can test each one today, the same way every time.

sentences: Scout doesn't need Orbit's real systems to be built and tested.
A small JSON file in the data folder holds the five sample orders, each with the customer's email.
Grace's boots were delivered 62 days ago, so she's a ready-made late return.
One tracking number always times out, so you can test what Scout does when the carrier fails.
And a stock dictionary lets you decide what is in stock and what isn't.
With fake data, every hard case happens on demand, the same way every time.

slides.title: One description, two outcomes

left.label: Before: ID only
points: Scout puts the email in order_id

right.label: After: ID or email
points: Description says when to use each
Scout passes the email as email

sentences: A tool description is an instruction the model reads every time it decides what to do.
Scout's first get order tool only took an order number.
But many customers write in with nothing but their email address.
With nowhere else to put it, Scout passed the email as an order number, got an error, and guessed.
The fixed tool takes an order number or an email, and its description says when to use each.
Now Scout passes the email in the right field and gets the real order.
You'll meet this exact bug again later in this module.

slides.title: Memory: pinned facts
slides.definition: Key details kept apart from the chat history, so trimming old messages never loses them.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A sticky note on your monitor: the chat scrolls away, but the note stays in view.

sentences: Scout's memory works the way you built it in Module 4, with pinned facts at its heart.
When a customer mentions an order number, Scout pins it.
Now it pins their email address too.
And once get order finds the order, Scout pins the customer's name.
Think of a sticky note on your monitor.
The chat scrolls away, but the note stays in view.

slides.title: Memory on every turn

note.text: Trim the chat, never the facts.

sentences: Here is what happens to memory on every turn.
A new message arrives from the customer.
Any order number or email in it is pinned as a fact.
The last ten customer turns are kept, and older ones are trimmed.
Scout sees the system prompt, the pinned facts and those recent turns.
Its final reply is saved as a turn, while the tool calls behind it stay inside that run.
The rule is simple: trim the chat, never the facts.

slides.title: Recap

points.text: Four tools look things up; two act, with rules inside the tool.
Fake data lets you test every hard case on demand.
A tool's description decides how the model uses it.
Pinned facts survive trimming: order ID, email, name.

sentences: Let's recap.
Scout has six tools: four that look things up, and two that act, with their rules inside the tool.
Fake data lets you make every hard case happen, whenever you want.
A tool's description is an instruction, and one sentence in it can fix a whole family of failures.
And pinned facts keep the order number, email and name safe while old turns are trimmed.
Next: what to do when Scout gets something wrong.

midQuiz.q: Which of Scout's tools needs a safety rule built into the tool itself, not just a line in the prompt?
midQuiz.explain: request_refund moves money. With the over-200-dollar approval rule inside the tool, a confused model still can't approve a big refund on its own.
midQuiz.hint: Which tool changes something instead of only reading?

midQuiz.q: Why does tools.py make one tracking number always time out?
options: So you can test what Scout does when the carrier fails
Because ParcelPath charges for every call
To slow Scout down so it thinks harder
midQuiz.explain: Fake data lets you make hard cases happen on demand. A guaranteed timeout tests Scout's error handling on every run, the same way each time.
midQuiz.hint: Which case would be hardest to catch with a real carrier?

endQuiz.q: Many customers give an email instead of an order number. What change helps Scout most?
options: Tell customers to find their order number first
Let get_order take an email, and say so in its description
Remove get_order and let the model answer from what it knows
endQuiz.explain: The model learns what a tool accepts from its schema and description. Give it a field for the email and say when to use it, and the error and the guess both go away.
endQuiz.hint: Where does the model learn what a tool accepts?

endQuiz.q: Thirty messages in, Scout's memory has trimmed the early turns. How does it still know the order number from message two?
options: It was pinned as a fact, and facts are never trimmed
The model remembers the whole chat on its own
It reads the order number back from the trace
endQuiz.explain: Trimming drops old turns, but pinned facts are added to every call. That is exactly what they are for.
endQuiz.hint: Think of the sticky note on the monitor.
